H1.text: A book on a tilted desk stays put, until one tilt too many. A sand pile never gets steeper than one slope.

H2.text: Something holds them, but only up to a limit.

H3.text: Aarav props up his drawing board, with his geometry box on it.

H4.text: He tilts it slowly. Still, still, then it shoots down. Two boxes taped together slip at the same angle. Why?

P2.text: Static friction pushes back just as hard as you push, but only up to a limit. That largest value, just before slipping, is limiting friction.

P4.text: Limiting friction equals mu s times N: the coefficient of static friction, times the normal force.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. A two kilogram block on a board, mu s zero point five.

S2.text: Tilt the board. The pull down the slope, m g sine theta, grows, and friction grows to match it.

S3.text: At ten degrees, both are three point four newtons. At twenty, six point seven.

S4.text: But the limit, mu s N, shrinks, as the block presses less into the board.

S5.text: At twenty six point six degrees, they meet. Friction is at its limit, eight point eight newtons.

S6.text: A hair more, and it slips. Kinetic friction, about seven newtons, takes over. The graph drops.

S7.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze at the moment of slipping.

S8.text: Down the slope, m g sine theta. Up the slope, friction at its limit. N balances m g cos theta. They are just equal.

D1.text: Now the rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. At rest, friction balances the pull down the slope. f equals m g sine theta.

D3.text: Step two. Into the slope, N equals m g cos theta.

D4.text: Step three. Static friction has a limit. f is at most mu s times N.

D5.text: Step four. About to slip: m g sine theta r equals mu s m g cos theta r.

D6.text: Step five. Cancel m g: tan theta r equals mu s. Theta r is the angle of repose.

T1.text: Remember this. At the angle of repose, tan theta equals mu s. The mass cancels out.

R1.text: Now, Aarav's puzzle. Link by link.

R2.text: A heavier box pulls harder down the slope.

R3.text: But it also presses harder, so N and the limit mu s N grow too.

R4.text: Both grow with m, in the same ratio. So m cancels.

K1.text: Side by side. At fifteen degrees, friction is five point one newtons, just m g sine theta. The limit is nine point five.

K2.text: At twenty six point six, friction reaches the limit. Static friction gives only what is needed.

K3.text: Your turn. At fifteen degrees, is the friction on the block nine point five newtons? Pause and decide.

K4.text: No! Only five point one. It reaches mu s N only at the point of slipping.

V1.text: One more pair. The angle of repose is the steepest slope where a body can rest. Tan theta r equals mu s.

V2.text: The angle of friction, lambda, is between N and the total contact force at the limit. Tan lambda equals f L over N, so it is mu s too.

V4.text: Now you try. Dry sand has mu s of zero point seven five. What is the steepest slope of a sand pile? Pause and decide.

V5.text: About thirty seven degrees! Tan thirty seven is about zero point seven five.

W2.text: Aarav presses a one point two kilogram book against a wall. Mu s is zero point four. What is the smallest push that holds it up?

W3.text: The weight is one point two times nine point eight. Eleven point seven six newtons.

W4.text: Friction must hold that up, and here N is the push F.

W5.text: At the limit, mu s F equals eleven point seven six. So F is eleven point seven six over zero point four.

W6.text: Twenty nine point four newtons. Any less, and the book slides.

X2.text: Many students say slipping starts when tan theta equals mu k.

X3.text: But a resting body slips when static friction runs out. So tan theta r equals mu s. Mu k matters only once it moves.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Bodies about to slip, on slopes and against walls.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A five kilogram block is on a thirty seven degree incline, mu s zero point five. g is ten, sine thirty seven is zero point six. What least force along the incline just starts it moving up? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Fifty newtons.

A2.text: Down the slope, m g sine theta is thirty newtons. N is forty.

A3.text: Moving up, limiting friction acts down the slope: twenty newtons.

A4.text: So F is thirty plus twenty, fifty. Ten newtons only stops it sliding down.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why do a light and a heavy box of one material slip at the same angle?

Y3.text: Two. Is static friction always equal to mu s N? When is it?

Y4.text: Three. What is the angle of friction, and why does it equal the angle of repose?

N1.text: Next time: why is a heavy box so much easier to move on wheels? Rolling friction.
